sweep_summary: Yucuna (yucu1253) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Robayo Romero 2018 (Forma y Función, open access, already held by the project), is directly about word prominence: an instrumental study showing that the Schauers' 'phonemic stress' marks track f0 rather than intensity, that words carry more than one prominence, and that Yukuna is better analysed as a two-tone language with lexically tone-specified roots and suffixes (pp.35, 39-44, 58-60). I also read the four other first-hand sources held by the project (Schauer & Schauer 1967 and 1978 stress analysis: phonemic, 1-3 stresses per word, intrinsic vs nonintrinsic stress shifting onto suffixes; Lemus Serrano 2020 PhD sec.1.2 and Lemus-Serrano et al. 2021 Glossa sec.2: restricted privative H-tone system, obligatory but not culminative) and newly downloaded Schauer & Schauer 1972 'Fonología del yucuna' (SIL 18919, via a 2024 Internet Archive copy; All sources agree that prominence is lexical and positionally unpredictable; the modern sources code it as tone, not stress. Best statement: Lemus-Serrano et al. 2021 p.3. Not obtained: Lemus Serrano 2016 MA (stress analysis, not on HAL), Ramirez 2001 p.359, Schauer & Schauer 2000 (no PDF) — all low priority since superseded by the 2018-2021 work. only direct downloads were possible.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No predictable word stress: word-level prominence is a lexically located H tone (privative H vs. zero, 'pitch accent'-like restricted tone). Every root carries one underlying /H/ (spreads one syllable rightward) or /HL/ (non-spreading), bound to a lexically specified syllable or floating onto following toneless material; most affixes are toneless, so surface H position shifts under suffixation. The position of H within the root is not predictable from word edges or weight (attested root patterns 2σ HH/HL/LH, 3σ HHL/LHH/HLL/LLH/LHL). Earlier SIL descriptions (Schauer & Schauer 1967: 65-68; 1978: 10-13) described the same facts as phonemic (lexical) stress with 'intrinsic' vs 'nonintrinsic' stress and regular shifts: nonintrinsic stress on the final stem syllable of verbs shifting to the following suffix syllable, and on the first syllable of disyllabic nouns shifting to the possessive suffix.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Modern analysis: none (a second surface H results from /H/ spreading; HLH second H lowered by downdrift). Schauer & Schauer 1978: 11 speak of a primary accent (higher pitch and intensity, usually on the base) and a secondary accent occurring only on affixes; 1967: 66 'Yucuna appears to have a multiple stress system' with up to three stresses per word.
new_statements.exceptions: Purposive suffix /-tʃí/ (and /-ɾé/) carry their own H unlike other (toneless) affixes; some irregular paradigms remain unexplained (Glossa sec. 5). Schauer & Schauer 1967: 68 note intrinsic stress on verb affixes -la, -ra, -he; 1978: 12 rare accent shift across a word boundary.
new_statements.domain_note: Root/word-level lexical tone; Glossa data are verb paradigms (80 roots x ~30 affix combinations) recorded in non-final position in a frame sentence, Leticia 2017-18, validated with other speakers; Robayo Romero 2018 shows instrumentally that f0, not intensity or duration, is the correlate of the prominence the Schauers wrote as stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language, Yucuna/Yukuna (yucu1253, ISO ycn), spoken on the Mirití-Paraná (Amazonas, Colombia) and by migrants in Leticia; speakers include ethnic Matapí whose original language is lost (Schauer & Schauer 1967: 62). Self-designation kamejeya. No dialect split is reported. Note the analytical split: SIL sources (1967, 1972, 1978) = lexical/phonemic stress with morphological shifts; Robayo Romero 2018 and Lemus Serrano 2020/2021 = restricted privative tone (H vs zero), i.e. the same lexical prominence reanalysed as tone.

new_statements.quote: Yukuna's word-prosodic system can be described as a restricted tonal system of the privative type, where H tone contrasts with the absence of tone. Such system corresponds to what is commonly labeled as 'pitch accent'. However, we avoid the latter term, following the property-driven typological phonology approach (Hyman 2009). In addition to having a limited tonal inventory (H vs. absence of H), Yukuna also displays low tonal density, in terms of the number and distribution of surface H syllables. When roots are produced without affixes, the following distributional rules apply: i) each root has at least one H syllable (e.g. *LLL), ii) each root has at most two H syllables (e.g. *HHH), iii) if there are two H tones, they are obligatorily adjacent (e.g. *HLH).
new_statements.citation: Lemus-Serrano, Magdalena, Marc Allassonnière-Tang & Dan Dediu (2021). What conditions tone paradigms in Yukuna: phonological and machine learning approaches. Glossa 6(1): 60, 1-22. doi:10.5334/gjgl.1276
new_statements.locator: sec.2 'The phonology of Yukuna's tonal system', p.3 (PDF p.3)
new_statements.reading: Yukuna has no positional word stress. Word-level prominence is a lexically specified privative H tone (underlying /H/ spreading vs /HL/ non-spreading vs toneless syllables), obligatory (at least one H per word) but not strictly culminative (up to two adjacent H), with lexically unpredictable position and complex, partly irregular interaction with suffixes. This is the current consensus of the three first-hand modern sources (Robayo 2018 instrumental study, Lemus Serrano 2020 thesis, Lemus-Serrano et al. 2021); the older SIL analysis (Schauer & Schauer 1967/1972/1978) called the same phenomenon 'phonemic stress' with 'intrinsic' (lexically fixed, any stem syllable) vs 'nonintrinsic' (stem-final in verbs, initial in disyllabic nouns, shifting onto suffixes) types and 1-3 stresses per word. on the catalog's classification: lexical/unpredictable prominence (tone-accent), not a fixed-position stress system.

new_statements.quote: 13.1.4. El acento. El acento es fonemático, como demuestran las siguientes oposiciones: /'hiɲa/ 'pez' /hi'ɲa/ diablo' /pa'taʔa/ 'trate (Ud.)' /pataʔ'a/ 'robe (Ud.)' Cada palabra en yucuna lleva, por lo menos, un acento primario. Puede llevar acento múltiple. Generalmente la raíz lleva el acento primario, pero éste puede trasladarse a los afijos, mientras que el acento secundario se da sólo en los afijos. Las palabras polisílabas pueden llevar de uno a tres acentos. [p.517] ... 13.2.1 Traslado de acento. El acento primario de las palabras es de dos clases: intrínseco (no cambia cuando lleva afijos) y extrínseco (puede cambiar cuando lleva afijos). El acento intrínseco lo puede llevar cualquier sílaba de la raíz, y no cambia. En los verbos, el acento extrínseco aparece sólo en las sílabas al final de la raíz. Al añadir afijos, éste suele trasladarse a la sílaba siguiente. [p.517]
new_statements.translation: 13.1.4. Stress. Stress is phonemic, as the following oppositions show: /'hiɲa/ 'fish' vs /hi'ɲa/ 'devil'; /pa'taʔa/ 'try (you, polite)' vs /pataʔ'a/ 'steal (you, polite)'. Every word in Yucuna carries at least one primary stress. It may carry multiple stress. Generally the root carries the primary stress, but it may shift onto the affixes, whereas secondary stress occurs only on affixes. Polysyllabic words may carry from one to three stresses. ... 13.2.1 Stress shift. The primary stress of words is of two kinds: intrinsic (does not change when the word takes affixes) and extrinsic (may change when it takes affixes). Intrinsic stress may be carried by any syllable of the root, and does not change. In verbs, extrinsic stress appears only on the syllables at the end of the root. When affixes are added, it usually shifts to the following syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is described as phonemic (contrastive) and lexically placed: 'intrinsic' stress may sit on any root syllable and is fixed, while 'extrinsic' stress sits on the root-final syllable in verbs (not restricted to root-final in nouns) and shifts onto the following affix syllable when suffixes are added, or in some cases onto the preceding syllable when a glottal-stop morpheme replaces the root-final syllable (p.518). Every word has at least one primary stress; words may carry one to three stresses; a few unaffixed words carry two primary stresses (/maka'pu'kuʧini/ 'round (flat objects)', /wali'hi'maka/ 'boy'); reduplicated portions repeat the same stress pattern.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress occurs only on affixes ('el acento secundario se da sólo en los afijos'); e.g. in verbs affixes can carry secondary stress when the root has intrinsic stress (/i'no-làʧa/ 'he did not kill').
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns: extrinsic stress is not limited to root-final syllable (/'peru/ 'axe' vs /nuperu'ne/ 'my axe'; /lu'ma/ vs /nuluma're/), contrasted with intrinsic-stress nouns (/li'ɲeru/, /nuli'ɲerute/). Extrinsic stress usually shifts to the syllable after the root but sometimes to the preceding syllable when a glottal-stop morpheme replaces the root-final syllable (/pa'ʔu-kaʔala/ 'four (round)', /pu'ra-kaʔalo-hi/ 'voice/word'). Some unaffixed words carry two primary stresses.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Yucuna of the Mirití-Paraná river, Amazonas, Colombia (the 2000 sketch says most of the 1,000-1,200 Yucuna live along the Mirití-Paraná and gives the language name as meaning 'story/news'); no separate dialect is named. The 1967 chapter is the English original of the SIL analysis later published in Spanish (1972 Fonología del yucuna, already held by the project) and restated in the 1978 grammar and this 2000 sketch.

new_statements.quote: 5. Suprasegmental phonemes. Stress is phonemic as shown by the following words: /vira/ 'he saws' /rira/ 'his blood' /piyuke/ 'old' /piyuke/ 'all' [p.65] Stress is not limited to one syllable per word. Rather, Yucuna appears to have a multiple stress system [p.66] ... 6.6. Stress. In relation to words, stress appears to be of two types: intrinsic and nonintrinsic. Various patterns of stress shift occur according to the interaction of these two stress types. The full system has not yet been worked out, but a few observations can be made. Intrinsic stress in general is nonperturbable and may cause stress perturbation. Nonintrinsic stress is perturbable. Either stress type is found both on stems and affixes. In verbs nonintrinsic stress occurs only on final stem syllable. The shift of stress is regularly to the syllable following the stem. Intrinsic stress may occur on any stem syllable. On verb affixes there appears to be intrinsic stress on -la, -ra, and -he. In two-syllable nouns nonintrinsic stress falls on the first syllable. With such nouns there is shift of stress to the possessive suffix. [pp.67-68]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (minimal pairs differing only in stress position) and words may carry more than one stress. Two types: intrinsic stress (lexically fixed, on any stem syllable, not perturbed by affixation) and nonintrinsic stress (stem-final in verbs, initial in disyllabic nouns, shifting onto the following suffix or the possessive suffix). The authors say the full system had not yet been worked out.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not distinguished as such in the 1967 text; 'multiple stress system' with more than one stress per word; intrinsic stress noted on verb affixes -la, -ra, -he.
new_statements.exceptions: 'The full system has not yet been worked out'; stress-shift patterns depend on the interaction of intrinsic and nonintrinsic stress; nouns vs verbs differ in where nonintrinsic stress sits.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe the Yucuna of the Mirití-Paraná river, Amazonas, Colombia (the 2000 sketch says most of the 1,000-1,200 Yucuna live along the Mirití-Paraná and gives the language name as meaning 'story/news'); no separate dialect is named. The 1967 chapter is the English original of the SIL analysis later published in Spanish (1972 Fonología del yucuna, already held by the project) and restated in the 1978 grammar and this 2000 sketch.

readall_conflicts: The two SIL works (Schauer & Schauer 1967 in Waterhouse ed., and Schauer & Schauer 2000) describe Yukuna word prominence as phonemic, lexically placed stress (intrinsic stress on any root syllable; extrinsic/nonintrinsic stress root-final in verbs, shifting onto suffixes; one to three stresses per word). The modern instrumental and phonological sources already in the catalog (Robayo 2018, Lemus Serrano 2020, Lemus-Serrano et al. 2021) reanalyse the same facts as a privative H-tone system ('restricted tonal system', pitch accent-like) rather than stress. This is a difference of analysis (stress vs privative tone) over the same lexically unpredictable prominence, not a disagreement about position: no source claims fixed positional word stress. Between the SIL works themselves there is no conflict; the 2000 sketch renames 'nonintrinsic' as 'extrínseco', adds that secondary stress occurs only on affixes, that a few unaffixed words carry two primary stresses, and that the extrinsic stress can shift leftwards before a glottal-stop morpheme.

sources.quote: In Yukuna, pitch variations are lexically distinctive, that is to say, there are pairs of segmentally identical words that can be distinguished through their respective pitch patterns. Phonetically, there are three pitch levels at play: low, mid and high, whilst phonemically, only two levels are contrastive: low (L) and high (H). ... Yukuna's word prosodic system can be described as a 'restricted' tonal system, or what is commonly called a 'pitch accent' system. ... All roots are specified for tone, while most affixes are toneless. [pp.8-9]
sources.note: Ch. sketch sec. 1 (p. 5-6): 'the tonal system (previously analyzed as a stress system)'. Sec. 1.2 Prosody (pp. 8-9): pitch is lexically distinctive; two contrastive levels; restricted tonal system 'or what is commonly called a pitch accent system' (term avoided); two phonemic H tones /H/ spreading and /HL/ non-spreading, no phonemic L, toneless syllables default L; all roots specified for tone, most affixes toneless; table of attested root tone patterns (1σ H; 2σ HH, HL, LH; 3σ HHL, LHH, HLL, LLH, LHL; *LLL, *HHH, *HLH). No separate word stress is described.

sources.quote: El acento es fonémico como se puede mostrar en las siguientes palabras: /virá/ 'él serrucha' /víra/ 'la sangre (de él)' ... Las polisílabas pueden tener de uno a tres acentos. En los verbos, el acento extrínseco ocurre solo en sílabas finales de raíz. El traslado del acento es regularmente a la sílaba que sigue a la raíz. sources.quote: Más de un acento primario por palabra contradice la definición de acento (Garde, 1968; Hyman, 2006), lo que invita a revisar los datos y a explorar otras interpretaciones. [p.35] ... sources.note: Instrumental (Praat) study of inflected verbs in frame sentences with two speaker pairs from the Mirití-Paraná: tests Schauer & Schauer's (1978: 11-13) phonemic-stress claims; intensity peaks do not align with their accent marks and duration is independent of pitch; f0 contour is the relevant cue; proposes Yukuna is tonal (two levels, alto/bajo) rather than accentual, with root tone patterns and tonal polarity on the first post-root suffix. Notes that 'more than one primary accent per word contradicts the definition of stress'.

sources.citation: Schauer, Stanley & Junia G. Schauer (1967). Yucuna phonemics. In V. G. Waterhouse (ed.), Phonemic Systems of Colombian Languages (SIL Publications in Linguistics 14), 61-71. Norman: SIL/Univ. of Oklahoma.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Stress is phonemic as shown by the following words: /rirá/ 'he saws' /rír a/ 'his blood' ... Stress is not limited to one syllable per word. Rather, Yucuna appears to have a multiple stress system [pp.65-66] ... In relation to words, stress appears to be of two types: intrinsic and nonintrinsic. ... Intrinsic stress in general is nonperturbable and may cause stress perturbation. Nonintrinsic stress is perturbable. ... In verbs nonintrinsic stress occurs only on final stem syllable. The shift of stress is regularly to the syllable following the stem. Intrinsic stress may occur on any stem syllable. ... In two-syllable nouns nonintrinsic stress falls on the first syllable. With such nouns there is shift of stress to the possessive suffix. [pp.67-68]
sources.note: Earliest first-hand description (fieldwork 1963-65): stress phonemic (minimal pairs), multiple stresses per word, two stress types (intrinsic = lexically fixed, any stem syllable; nonintrinsic = stem-final in verbs, initial in disyllabic nouns, shifting rightward onto suffixes). 'The full system has not yet been worked out.' Reanalyzed as tone by Robayo 2018 and Lemus Serrano 2020/2021.
